OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Correctly recognize a spinal cord injury and the forms of shock that may occur after spinal
injury.
Identify imaging studies indicated in evaluating traumatic spine injuries.
Apply criteria for evaluation of the cervical spine.
Develop a safe and effective algorithm for the timing of the management of spinal injuries.
Overview
Spinal trauma may be complex, ranging from multiple injuries in polytrauma patients to
isolated injury.
Timely diagnosis and initial management of spinal trauma are essential in optimizing
outcomes and avoiding catastrophic sequelae of undetected or underestimated spine injuries.

Epidemiology
The true incidence of spinal trauma is difficult to quantify; however, the incidence of spinal
trauma appears to be increasing and will continue to increase based on current population
trends.
Overall, spinal fractures are three times more likely to occur in males.
Osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures are more common in females.

Epidemiology
The true incidence of spinal trauma is unknown, namely for two reasons. First, inclusion
criteria differ across registries; therefore, population-level estimates are inherently
flawed. Second, an existing number of patients with spinal trauma are never captured.
For example, 10% to 20% of patients with a spinal cord injury die before reaching a
hospital; therefore, these injuries are not included in the incidence of spinal trauma.
However, the incidence of spinal trauma appears to be increasing; this is the result of an
aging population and the increasing prevalence of osteoporosis. In the United States,
more than 2 million new osteoporotic fractures occur each year. The most common type
of osteoporotic fracture is a vertebral compression fracture, which is associated with an
estimated incidence ranging from 700,000 to 750,000 annually.
Spinal trauma places a short- and long-term functional burden on the patient and the
healthcare system. Certain spinal fractures are associated with a considerable mortality
risk. Harris et al1 reported a 28% 1-year mortality rate in patients older than 65 years
who had a cervical spine fracture. This 1-year mortality rate increased to 39% in patients
older than 85 years.
Given the rising incidence in spinal trauma in the geriatric population, an increase in
healthcare expenditures is expected. These increased expenses are the result of direct
costs (eg, emergency room visit, imaging studies, posthospitalization needs) and indirect
costs (eg, lost time at work by patient and family members involved in care). In depth
analysis has shown that 75% of all healthcare expenditures were actually incurred
because of a patient’s comorbidities rather than the osteoporotic fracture itself. This

Evaluation of Spinal Trauma
Assessment in the Field
Because of the potential for catastrophic neurologic injury, especially in patients who sustain
high-energy trauma, an unstable spine injury should be assumed until proven otherwise.
If a patient can communicate immediately postinjury, then information should be gathered
regarding the mechanism of injury; the presence of neck or back pain; and any weakness,
numbness, or pain in the extremities.
If an injury is suspected, then the cervical spine should be immobilized in a rigid cervical
collar, and the patient should be transported on a firm spine board with lateral support
devices.

Assessment in the Field
Because of the potential for catastrophic neurologic injury, especially in patients who
sustain high-energy trauma, an unstable spine injury should be assumed until proven
otherwise. If a patient can communicate immediately postinjury, information should be
gathered regarding the mechanism of injury; the presence of neck or back pain; and any
weakness, numbness, or pain in the extremities. If an injury is suspected, then the
cervical spine should be immobilized in a rigid cervical collar, and the patient should be
transported on a firm spine board with lateral support devices.
If a patient is unresponsive or obtunded, then spinal precautions should be
implemented. The Glasgow Coma Scale is an evaluation tool used to determine a
patient’s neurologic status based on their alertness, orientation, and motor response2
(Figure 1). Neurologic status can be monitored by comparing a patient’s initial Glasgow
Coma Scale score with subsequent assessments. Adequate spinal immobilization, if
indicated, should begin in the field.3 Although providers should always err on the side of
caution, the National Association of Emergency Medical Services Physicians and the

American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma does not recommend spinal
immobilization if a patient has a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15, has no spinal
tenderness or neurologic complaints, has no distracting injuries, and is not intoxicated.4
Prolonged immobilization on a spine board may result in pain, pressure sores, and
impaired respiration and, therefore, may be detrimental to patients without a traumatic
spine injury (Figure 2). Failure to follow protocols in the assessment of trauma patients
in the field may lead to disastrous complications. Toscano3 reported that inadequate
immobilization led to worsening of neurologic injury in as many as 25% of patients.

Assessment in the Emergency Room
A stepwise and complete evaluation of the spine should be performed, regardless of patient
presentation, to ensure no injuries are missed.
Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) is a protocol established by the American College of
Surgeons to guide the evaluation of trauma patients in the emergency room, including the safe
and efficient identification of spinal injuries.

Assessment in the Emergency Room
ATLS is a protocol established by the American College of Surgeons to guide the
evaluation of trauma patients in the emergency room, including the safe and efficient
identification of life-threatening conditions and the determination of appropriate initial
treatment.5 The ATLS evaluation includes a primary survey, resuscitation, and a
secondary survey.
Primary Survey
The primary survey involves critical assessment of the airway, breathing, and circulation.
Hemorrhagic shock is the most common form of shock in trauma patients; however, in
patients with a spinal cord injury, clinicians must be able to recognize features of neurogenic
or spinal shock because they are associated with different treatment approaches.


Primary Survey
The primary survey involves critical assessment of the airway, breathing, and circulation.
A spinal injury rarely will directly compromise an airway or prevent intubation. In
addition, breathing is commonly affected by blunt trauma to the chest, such as a
pneumothorax or hemothorax; however, spinal cord injuries may affect respiratory
performance. Spinal cord injuries above the C5 level may result in diaphragm paralysis,
and patients with such an injury are more likely to require intubation. In addition,
intubation is more likely with complete quadriplegia compared with incomplete
quadriplegia or paraplegia. A spinal cord injury at any level may affect the intercostal
thoracic muscles and abdominal muscle tone, which may increase the effort of
breathing, thereby resulting in mechanical ventilation dependence. In such patients,
continuous respiratory monitoring in the form of arterial blood gases and vital capacity
is recommended. If intubation is deemed necessary to maintain an airway and breathing
in a patient in whom a cervical spine injury is known or suspected, then immobilization
must be maintained in the form of a rigid cervical collar or via manual in-line
mobilization as the cervical collar is temporarily removed.
Patients with a spinal cord injury may present with varying manifestations of shock,
including neurogenic shock or spinal shock. Clinicians must be able to differentiate
neurogenic from spinal shock because they are associated with different treatment
approaches. Neurogenic shock is a form of distributive shock that occurs if a spinal cord
injury interrupts the sympathetic input on peripheral vasculature and the heart. A
patient with impaired sympathetic tone and an intact parasympathetic nervous system
typically has hypotension (systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg) and bradycardia.
Bradycardia is the factor that distinguishes neurogenic shock from hemorrhagic shock.
Neurogenic shock is most common in patients with a spinal cord injury above the T4
level and is observed in approximately 20% of all patients with a cervical spinal cord
injury. Complete spinal cord injuries also are associated with a higher incidence of
neurogenic shock than incomplete spinal cord injuries.
Spinal shock, which is distinctly different in etiology than neurogenic shock, refers to loss
of neurologic function within the first 24 to 48 hours after spinal cord injury and is
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:39 AM
AAOS | Spinal Evaluation in the Trauma Patient
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000054
6/21

thought to result from the temporary physiologic state of an acutely traumatized spinal
cord. Because the peripheral nerves are unresponsive to brain stimuli, spinal shock
manifests as the transient absence of reflexes, motor function, and sensory function
caudal to the spinal cord injury. Dissimilar from neurogenic shock, blood pressure and
heart rate are not affected. Typically, spinal shock ends within 24 to 48 hours of injury,
with gradual return of the bulbocavernosus reflex, which is the lowest spinal cord–
mediated reflex. Theoretically, a complete spinal cord injury cannot be diagnosed until
the bulbocavernosus reflex returns, indicating the end of spinal shock.
Resuscitation
Correction of hypotension in trauma patients, regardless of the cause, is critical to maintain
organ perfusion and minimize secondary ischemic injury to the spinal cord.

Resuscitation
Most trauma patients, even those with a spinal cord injury, have hypotension as a result
of blood loss. If a patient remains hypotensive after volume repletion, then neurogenic
shock should be strongly suspected. The next step in management includes
vasopressors, such as dopamine and norepinephrine. These are a-agonists that increase
systemic vascular resistance. If bradycardia persists, then atropine should be
administered to increase cardiac output. Lastly, temporary pacing may be required.
Management of shock does not end in the emergency room. Although many trauma
patients will be admitted to the intensive care unit because of injury burden, admission
to the intensive care unit is recommended for patients with a spinal cord injury to
prevent secondary spinal cord injury from hypoperfusion. Unless contraindicated, a
mean arterial pressure greater than 90 mm Hg should be maintained for 1 week after a
spinal cord injury to avoid episodes of hypotension (systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg).

Performing the log rolling maneuver while maintaining cervical immobilization allows for
inspection of dorsal spine anatomy from the occiput to the sacrum and positions the patient
for digital rectal examination. (Figure 3)
In a stable patient who is alert and responsive, a thorough neurologic examination, including
motor and sensory testing, should be performed.
Figure 3 Illustrations show the steps for the log roll maneuver. (Reproduced from Kwon BK,
Bourassa-Moreau E: Initial management of the patient with spine trauma, in Truumees E, Prather
H, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Spine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 383-393.)

Secondary Survey
After the airway, breathing, and circulation are stabilized, the secondary survey is
initiated. This portion of the ATLS protocol is a stepwise method for the evaluation of
injuries and the selection of imaging studies.

If the log rolling maneuver is performed, the spine board used to transport the patient
should be removed. Prolonged immobilization on a spine board may result in pressure
sores, particularly in patients without protective sensation. Visual and manual inspection
of the spine includes palpation for tenderness, step-off, and crepitus and identification
of any ecchymosis or lesions. These findings may indicate fractures or disruption of the
posterior ligamentous complex. The mechanism of injury also may aid in the diagnosis of
a spinal injury. Thoracic spinal injuries are commonly observed in motorcyclists, whereas
flexion-distraction injuries are associated with seat-belt injuries during motor vehicle
accidents. In addition, lower extremity injuries secondary to axial loading, such as
calcaneus fractures, should increase suspicion for a thoracolumbar burst fracture.
The American Spinal Injury Association classification is a thorough method for identifying
neurologic deficits in trauma patients (Figure 4). The motor component of the physical
examination evaluates the strength of five key upper and five key lower muscle groups
and is graded on a scale ranging from 0 to 5. In addition, voluntary anal contraction
should be assessed and recorded as present or absent. The sensory component of the
physical examination evaluates 28 dermatomes, with S4-S5 being the most caudal
dermatome. Sensation is scored as 0, 1 or 2, indicating absent, impaired, or normal
sensation, respectively. The examiner must be cognizant of injuries to the extremities
that may compromise assessment and whether a patient is in distress or affected by
medications. In addition, a complete spinal cord injury cannot be diagnosed if a patient
is in spinal shock, and the bulbocavernosus reflex must be allowed to return before such
a diagnosis is made. Because of these confounding factors, the American Spinal Injury
Association Impairment Scale score is inaccurate within the first 72 hours of an injury,
emphasizing the importance of repeat examinations.

Figure 4 Image shows the International Standards for the Neurologic Classification of
Spinal Cord Injury (ISNCSCI; formerly American Spinal Injury Association [ASIA]) and ASIA
Impairment Scale (AIS). The documentation of motor and sensory function and
determination of the severity of paralysis is critical for patients with spinal cord injuries.
The ISNCSCI motor score is comprised of the strength in 10 key muscle groups, whereas
the sensory score for light touch and pinprick is comprised of sensation within 28
dermatomes. Testing of perianal sensation and anal contraction is critical to determine
whether any function has been preserved in the lowest sacral segments, S4-S5.
Assignment of an AIS grade is based on these neurologic findings. Note that on sensory
testing, the C4 dermatome extends in a cape-like distribution down the proximal part of
the thorax. (Reproduced with permission from the American Spinal Injury Association.
Available at: http://asia-spinalinjury.org.)

Imaging Modalities
The National Emergency X-Radiography Utilization Study (NEXUS) and the Canadian C-Spine
Rule (CCR) are two guidelines that aid in determining if cervical spine imaging studies are
necessary after blunt trauma (Figures 5 and 6).
CT is associated with a 99% sensitivity for the detection of cervical spine injuries and is
recommended as the primary imaging modality for evaluation of the cervical spine by the
Eastern Association for the Surgery of Trauma.6
MRI is not recommended for evaluating spinal trauma but may provide useful and diagnostic
information on soft-tissue injuries, the intervertebral disks, and neurologic deficits.
Figure 5 Image shows the Canadian C-Spine Rule (Reproduced with permission from Stiell IG,
Clement CM, McKnight RD, et al: The Canadian C-spine rule versus the NEXUS low-risk criteria in
patients with trauma. N Engl J Med 2003;349[26]:2510-2518.)

Imaging Modalities
The NEXUS and the CCR are two guidelines that aid in determining if cervical spine
imaging studies are necessary after blunt trauma. If imaging of the cervical spine is
deemed necessary based on the initial assessment, then CT is the preferred imaging
modality. Plain radiography is of low utility in assessing for spinal trauma because it
frequently results in missed spinal injuries and because of the availability and efficiency
of CT and MRI.

The rate of false-negative results with regard to the detection of spinal injuries via plain
radiography alone is 30% in the cervical spine, 52% in the thoracic spine, and 14% in the
lumbar spine. Plain radiographs are associated with inferior details compared with CT
scans and cannot completely capture the occipitocervical and craniocervical junctions. In
addition, CT scans provide information regarding the surrounding vasculature. CT
angiography is recommended if a basilar or vertebral artery injury is suspected.
Distinctive signs of vertebral artery injury include blurred vision, vertigo, or altered
consciousness; however, most patients with a unilateral vertebral artery injury are
asymptomatic secondary to collateral circulation.
Clearing the Cervical Spine of Injury
The goal of a cervical spine evaluation is to rule out a cervical spine injury.
A standardized and thorough evaluation should be performed in every patient who sustains
blunt trauma to minimize the likelihood of missed injuries.
If midline cervical tenderness on palpation, pain with range of motion, neurologic deficits,
altered levels of consciousness, or distracting injuries are present, then the cervical spine is
not cleared, and CT is recommended. MRI may be considered as an adjunct.

Clearing the Cervical Spine of Injury
The goal of a cervical spine evaluation is to rule out a cervical spine injury. A
standardized and thorough evaluation should be performed in every patient who
sustains blunt trauma to minimize the likelihood of missed injuries.
The NEXUS and the CCR provide guidance with regard to indications for cervical spine
imaging. By following the proposed algorithms, an alert and asymptomatic patient can
be cleared based on clinical assessment alone, avoiding unnecessary imaging studies.
The cervical collar can be removed if the patient is awake, alert, not intoxicated, and
neurologically intact and has full, painless range of motion of the cervical spine. If
midline cervical tenderness on palpation, pain with range of motion, neurologic deficits,
altered levels of consciousness, or distracting injuries are present, then the cervical spine
is not cleared, and CT is recommended7 (Resource 1). Research has shown that the

NEXUS and the CCR are associated with a sensitivity of 99% and 100%, respectively, with
regard to ruling out cervical spine injuries.8,9
Although the threshold to clear the cervical spine of injury should be very high,
prolonged immobilization is associated with disadvantages. A rigid cervical collar is
associated with an increased risk of aspiration; decreased respiratory function;
intracranial hypertension; and the development of ulcers at collar pressure points, such
as the occiput and the submandibular area. These risks are higher in geriatric patients;
therefore, patients with a cervical collar should be closely monitored.
In an awake, alert patient without distracting injuries who is not intoxicated and is
cooperative with the complete physical examination, the cervical collar can be removed
after CT scans rule out cervical injuries.7 A similar yet more controversial approach can
be used in obtunded patients and patients who are intoxicated or have distracting
injuries. Controversy exists with regard to whether modern CT alone is sufficient to rule
out cervical spine injury or if MRI is necessary to assess for occult ligamentous injuries or
other types of subtle spinal trauma. MRI is a more sensitive imaging modality than CT;
however, many studies have questioned whether injuries identified via MRI that were
not visualized on CT are clinically important enough to warrant delayed cervical collar
removal.7 In a secondary review of the cervical CT scans of 91 patients cleared of injury
by radiologists, Simon et al10 reported a potential for occult trauma in 22 patients. In
addition, MRI identified injuries missed on CT scans in 17 of these 22 patients.
In a large-scale series of more than 8,000 patients evaluated for cervical spine injuries
between 2007 and 2014, Schoenfeld et al11 reported that the likelihood of identifying a
cervical spine injury was substantially higher in patients in whom CT and MRI was
obtained, even after adjusting for prior injury recognition on CT. MRI revealed injuries
not previously recognized on CT in 8% of the patients; a minority of these injuries were
serious enough to warrant surgical management. Therefore, the authors maintained
that the standard addition of MRI to CT-alone imaging protocols in evaluation of the
cervical spine after trauma could not be substantiated.
Should a decision be made to not obtain MRI, a best practice may involve asking multiple
practitioners from various services (eg, spine, trauma, radiology, etc.) to review CT scans

The Ankylosed Spine
Special attention should be paid to patients with conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis and
diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis because seemingly innocuous low-energy trauma may
result in unstable spinal column injuries with the potential for catastrophic neurologic injuries.
These patients cannot be cleared of injury via negative plain radiographs alone; therefore,
advanced imaging studies, including CT and MRI, should be obtained. (Figures 7 and 8)
Figure 7 Photographs show elderly patients with a fixed sagittal deformity. Ankylosing spondylitis
or another potentially stiff spine at risk for fracture should be assumed in patients with a head
that does not lay flat on a spine board; therefore, padding should be used, and the head should
be taped in a position of patient-directed comfort. (Reproduced from Oitment C, Thornley P,
Jentzsch T, Pahuta M: Damage control orthopaedics in spinal trauma. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2021;29[24]:e1291-e1302.)

The Ankylosed Spine
In patients with hyperostotic conditions, such as ankylosing spondylitis and diffuse
idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis, normal anatomy may be obscured, and segments may
be fused together via the pathologic process. Because the spinal segments are fused
together, a fracture through an ankylosed spine results in long lever arms, and the spinal
fracture behaves similar to a diaphyseal fracture in a long bone. Nondisplaced fractures
are particularly common in patients with an ankylosed spine and are associated with an
increased risk of displacing with movement. They also may be difficult to detect on plain
radiographs and CT scans.12
Therefore, clinicians must critically assess for ankylosis on imaging studies because
these fractures must be managed in a different manner than fractures in a non-

ankylosed spine. Strict spinal precautions should be maintained, with no attempts at
manipulation, until advanced imaging studies, including CT and MRI (if possible), are
performed (Resource 2). Neurologic evaluation also is required because patients may
deteriorate rapidly as a result of subtle changes in alignment of an otherwise unstable
spine and as a result of epidural hematoma. In a retrospective series of 112 patients with
spinal fractures in an ankylosed spine, Caron et al13 reported delayed diagnosis of spinal
fractures in 19% of the patients, 81% of whom experienced abrupt neurologic
deterioration before eventual identification of the fracture. Patients with fractures of the
ankylosed spine, even if nondisplaced, typically are treated via long-segment
instrumented fusion procedures that span the fracture site.
Identifying Noncontiguous Spine Injuries
The incidence of noncontiguous spine injuries in patients who sustain blunt trauma is high,
ranging from 3% to 16%.
CT of the entire spine generally is recommended if a vertebral column injury is identified in
patients who sustain high-energy trauma.

Identifying Noncontiguous Spine Injuries
The incidence of noncontiguous spine injuries in patients who sustain blunt trauma is
high, ranging from 3% to 16%. Noncontiguous spine injuries are associated with a higher
rate of spinal cord injuries, especially if they are missed during initial evaluation. A
thorough evaluation of all spinal regions from the occipitocervical junction to the sacrum
is necessary, if not already performed, if a single traumatic injury to the spine is
identified. CT of the entire spine generally is recommended if a vertebral column injury is
identified, especially in patients with a high-energy trauma mechanism of injury.
Acute Management of Spinal Trauma
Initial Closed Reduction

A traumatic cervical facet dislocation can be safely and effectively reduced via traction in a
patient who can reliably undergo repeat clinical assessments.
Closed reduction should not be attempted in patients who are unconscious or obtunded.
The decision to perform MRI of the cervical spine before closed reduction is controversial
because the maneuver may drag a herniated disk fragment into the spinal cord and result in
neurologic injury.

Initial Closed Reduction
A traumatic cervical facet dislocation can be safely and effectively reduced via traction in
a patient who can reliably undergo repeat clinical assessments. Closed reduction should
not be attempted in patients who are unconscious or obtunded. Weights are applied at
intervals via a traction device, and movement across the dislocated segments is regularly
assessed via fluoroscopic imaging. A clinical assessment should be performed after
every reduction attempt or after weights are added, and traction should be discontinued
immediately if a patient’s neurologic status worsens.
The decision to perform MRI of the spine before closed reduction is controversial
because the maneuver may drag a herniated disk fragment into the spinal cord and
result in neurologic injury. However, post-reduction MRI of the cervical spine should be
performed before surgical management.
Timing of Surgical Management
If spinal surgery is indicated, the timing of surgical management should include consideration
of the physiologic status of the patient, additional traumatic injuries, other comorbidities, and
risks associated with the administration of anesthesia.
The Surgical Timing in Acute Spinal Cord Injury Study established the recommendation that
surgical decompression for the management of acute spinal cord injuries should be
performed within 24 hours to optimize the likelihood of neurologic improvement.


Timing of Surgical Management
If spinal surgery is indicated, the timing of surgical management should be determined
by a multidisciplinary consultation team, including the trauma team, anesthesia service,
and other healthcare providers involved in the management of a patient’s injuries. A
decision regarding the timing of spinal surgery must consider the physiologic status of
the patient, additional traumatic injuries, other comorbidities, and risks associated with
the administration of anesthesia.
The Surgical Timing in Acute Spinal Cord Injury Study established the recommendation
that surgical decompression for the management of acute spinal cord injuries should be
performed within 24 hours to optimize the likelihood of neurologic improvement.14 The
Surgical Timing in Acute Spinal Cord Injury Study was a multicenter, prospective study
involving patients with a cervical spinal cord injury. The authors reported that 19.8% of
patients who underwent surgical or open decompression within 24 hours postinjury
experienced neurologic improvement (defined as at least a two grade American Spinal
Injury Association Impairment Scale improvement at 6-month follow-up) compared with
8.6% of patients who underwent surgical or open decompression more than 24 hours
postinjury.
